prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B041 with Katori and Ye as a single two-name part. Having read the full round-1 exchange, the scientific case rests on three points I can defend as an experimentalist. First, the invention is specific: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the trap light shift while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement, and that is not what combs (2005) or single-ion control (2012) did. Those prizes rewarded the ruler and the single quantum system. This one rewards the idea of interrogating a very large neutral-atom ensemble without disturbing the clock transition, which is why stability and systematics both improved. Second, it is confirmed in the way I ask of any claim: Sr, Yb and Hg lattice clocks in several countries agree in frequency ratios at the low 1e-18 level and are compared routinely. Third, it has already taught us something about nature, which answers the chair's own question and Lindroth's and Danielsson's objection: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre height differences, and tighter bounds on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings. No deviation from known physics has been seen, but a null result at that precision is a measurement of nature, and the same is true of many prizes I respect. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking the platform to record accuracy and stability. I would not add a third name; the PTB, SYRTE and NIST contributions are real but a three-name cap forces a cut, and I would word the citation around the lattice clock only, so that Ye's comb work, already honoured, is not re-credited. The still-pending redefinition of the second does not change the physics, which is already done and agreed between laboratories. The dates of the first strontium lattice clock and of the first 1e-18 evaluation, and the exact uncertainty values, must be verified against the published record before any citation is drafted. I quote them from memory.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is the one from members who ranked B041 seventh, Danielsson, Johansson and Mehlig: that this is a superb metrology achievement and a third clock-related prize, and not a discovery that changes our picture of the world. I do not think it is overlap in the sense of duplicating 2005 or 2012, but I accept that reasonable people weigh conceptual novelty above measurement capability, and then B032 is the stronger statement. A second reservation is credit: the lattice-clock race involved several groups, and two names will leave out Takamoto, Lemonde, Lisdat and others, and I cannot rule out that a careful historical review would show a different cut. Third, a nominally mature field whose headline practical use, the redefinition of the second, is still undecided is easier to criticise than a prize for a settled paradigm. Finally, the support is broad but shallow, and as Chair I do not treat that as evidence of merit.

responses.point: You asked, in effect, that B032 be decided on the basis of the trio, and you would drop Mele for Hasan, while stating that you could live with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. You also rank B041 seventh, and the chair's summary asks whether that is a scientific or an overlap objection.
responses.response: Your willingness to accept Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is helpful, because it shows that the one-name difference is a real but narrow dispute. I still find it telling that the committee has not converged, and that the 3D ARPES priority you flag is unverified by anyone here. If you say your seventh place is about overlap, I would answer that the magic-wavelength lattice with a many-atom ensemble is a distinct invention from the comb and ion prizes, and that the clocks have already produced millimetre-scale redshift and constraints on varying constants. If it is that no deviation from known physics has been found, I would ask whether that is a standard we apply to measurement prizes elsewhere. I will say plainly that if the committee chooses to settle the B032 attribution explicitly and cleanly, I would regard it as a respectable fallback and not as a poor outcome.

responses.point: Topological insulators are a new state of matter with quantitative agreement between ARPES, transport and first-principles theory, and the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is the coherent theory-plus-experiment configuration, with attribution as the main weakness.
responses.response: I accept your argument that the conceptual weight of B032 is larger than that of B041, and I accept that I am not the right person to judge Kane-Mele priority against Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang. The attribution problem is not only a matter of who is missing. The HgTe experiment was guided by a proposal by people outside every trio, which means that a prize for the experimental realisation rewards an experiment whose theoretical motivation is partly not credited. You ask in your own case against for what you would do if the chain is too contested to cut at three. I think that is the situation on the evidence we have now. If the committee can verify the chronology and a citation tied to the 2D quantum spin Hall state is defensible, I would move to B032 as my first alternative, which is where it already stands.

responses.point: You support B041 with a citation built on the magic wavelength, but worry that it could be read as an instrument achievement instead of a discovery, and you leave open whether a third lattice-clock name is needed.
responses.response: I agree with the citation wording and with the point that the new element is neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice. On your open third name, I have thought about it and I would hold at two. The candidates for a third name (Takamoto, Lemonde, Lisdat) each contributed to a part of the story, but none is the single clearly missing figure, and adding one would invite the same argument over the next. I would meet your concern about discovery by writing the citation to say what the lattice clock achieved and not just the number, so that relativistic and fundamental-physics tests appear as the reason for the prize.

responses.point: You prefer B032 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the one candidate where a clean model, a sharp prediction and a decisive experiment line up, and you rank B041 seventh because of its closeness to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: The case that B032 has the cleanest chain from model to prediction to experiment is a strong one and I agree with it on the physics. Where I differ is on the claim that the credit chain is then complete: your own case against says that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the Fu-Kane work are outside the trio. I also do not agree that B041 is a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. Those honoured the frequency comb and the control of single ions, while the lattice clock is a different object that rests on a different idea. I note that you list B041 as an alternative, so the question between us is the ordering of two candidates we both regard as mature.

responses.point: Circuit QED is a new regime of strong, tunable single-photon coupling with a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing, and you disclose that you are the member closest to the field and invite the committee to discount your ranking.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure and I would treat your ranking as informative about the physics while not counting it as decisive for the prize. I think the timing argument you yourself raise is a fair one: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is close, and Girvin and Huang co-authored the 2004 proposal, so the cut at three is contested. I am not able to judge the physics of circuit QED beyond what you describe, and I defer to you on its being a distinct regime. I do not think your proximity requires recusal, in the sense that you have no personal tie to the credited names, but I would ask you to say whether B041 is an acceptable fallback on scientific grounds.

responses.point: You regard B041 as a new measurement capability that has changed what can be observed, with Katori on the concept and Ye on performance, and you raise the pending redefinition of the second as a possible maturity condition.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the lineage. On maturity, I do not think the redefinition of the second should be a condition, since that decision depends on metrological agreement and on international bodies, and the physics we would be crediting does not depend on it. I would ask that you and I be careful to separate the two uses of the word mature. As to your own point about reading the uncertainty values from memory, it applies to me too, and I would support a verification step before the citation is drafted.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as a distinct discovery rather than a third metrology prize, which is the real divide between the B041 and B032 camps and cannot be settled by counting support.

The historical record: dates of the first strontium lattice clock and of the first 1e-18 evaluations, and whether Katori and Ye are a sufficient credit without a third name. I quote these from memory.
Whether the B032 attribution chain (Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu, Hasan) can be settled by checking chronology, in which case B032 may become the stronger prize.
Whether neutrino source identification (B033) is mature enough to be a candidate in a coming year. I have moved it out of my alternatives because it is in my own field and I judge it not yet secure.
How much weight the pending redefinition of the second should carry as a maturity condition.
statement.conflict_note: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations. B033 (IceCube neutrinos) is in my own astroparticle field and was my opening first choice, so I flag that proximity, although it is no longer among my alternatives and I know of no direct tie to Halzen or Karle. I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups, and no conflict for B041. As Chair, I have tried to state the B032 and B031 cases in their supporters' terms, but I prefer B041 and the committee should weigh my views on that basis.
